newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore assures Chinese premier over funding issue.
newsitem.headline: Gore assures Chinese premier over funding issue.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore assured Chinese Premier Li Peng on Tuesday that allegations China tried to illegally influence U.S. elections last year would not deflect Washington from a policy of engagement with Beijing.
A U.S. official who attended the meetings between Gore and Li said the Chinese premier raised the issue and vigorously denied the allegations of illegal payments to the U.S. Democratic Party.
Gore told Li the issue was being investigated "but the important point was that this in no way would deflect the administration from pursuing its policy of engagement with China", the official said.
Li responded by saying he was assured this would not affect Washington's pledges to improve ties with Beijing, the official added.
Discussion on the issue, which has cast a shadow over Gore's visit, lasted for several minutes.

The Washington Post has reported that the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned six members of Congress last year they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign funds from foreign corporations.
Gore launched his first full day in China with a series of high-level talks and is scheduled to meet Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Wednesday.
Members of the U.S. delegation said little had been done to bridge the gap between the two countries on human rights but talks on the issue were less acrimonious than in the past.
"We had a very productive and energetic talk," Gore told a news briefing in the Great Hall of the People after his talks with Li.

"The meetings today were very positive. Both sides have a desire to lend forward momentum...recognising areas where we agreed to disagree," said Gore, the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit China since then president George Bush in early 1989.
Gore and Li presided over signings of two multi-million dollar contracts for U.S. business in China, giving a sign that once chilly ties between Beijing and Washington were thawing.

Boeing Co signed a deal to sell five 777-200 aircraft worth $685 million to China's international carrier, Air China. General Motors Corp launched a long-delayed joint venture with Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp to build medium-sized cars.
Despite the good cheer created by the contracts, Li sounded a note of caution which reflected China's concern about growing U.S. influence in world affairs.

"We believe the United States, the biggest developed country in the world, should play a more positive role in international affairs," Li said. "The importance of our relations serves the interests of both peoples."
China appeared keen that disputes over human rights should not be allowed to overshadow business gains.
"There are in fact differences between China and the United States on some issues, including differences on human rights," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
"It would not be possible for there to be no differences between two such big nations with such contrasting cultures."
